result:
**Recommendation: don't split yet.** For five teams, a modular monolith (one deployable, hard internal boundaries) solves most of what micro-frontends promise at a fraction of the cost. Split only if you can name a specific pain that only independent deployment fixes, and then only carve out that piece.

I haven't seen your codebase or release process, so this rests on typical five-team setups; the conditions further down say when it flips.

## What micro-frontends buy you

- **Independent deploys:** a team ships without waiting on a shared release train or another team's broken build. This is the only benefit you can't get any other way.
- **Fault and blast-radius isolation:** a bad release from one team takes down its own section, not the whole app.
- **Stack autonomy:** teams can upgrade React or swap libraries on their own schedule. This is useful for incremental migration off legacy code, but otherwise mostly a liability.
- **Enforced boundaries:** the boundaries are physical, so nobody can casually import another team's internals.

## What they cost

- **Runtime complexity:** you take on a shell app, Module Federation or similar, version negotiation for shared dependencies, and failures that only appear at integration time in production.
- **Performance:** duplicated dependencies and extra network round-trips, unless you invest in sharing, which reintroduces coupling.
- **UX consistency:** design system versions drift across teams, and routing, auth, analytics and error handling all need contracts between apps.
- **Cross-cutting changes get harder:** a design-system bump or auth change becomes N coordinated releases instead of one PR.
- **Platform tax:** someone has to own the shell, CI templates, shared-dependency policy and local dev story. In practice that is one or two engineers permanently, or a sixth team.
- **Testing:** end-to-end tests across independently versioned pieces are slower and flakier than in a single app.

## Why the modular monolith usually wins at this size

Most "the monolith is slowing us down" complaints are really about ownership, build time or coupling. All three can be fixed in place:

| Pain | Fix without splitting |
|---|---|
| Teams step on each other | Per-team packages in a monorepo (Nx or Turborepo), CODEOWNERS, lint-enforced import boundaries |
| Slow CI | Affected-only builds and tests, remote caching |
| Risky shared releases | Feature flags, continuous deploy from trunk, route-level code splitting, per-route error boundaries |
| Unclear contracts | Explicit public APIs per package, with the design system as a versioned internal package |

This gets you the enforced boundaries and most of the autonomy, while keeping atomic cross-team refactors, one dependency graph and one thing to debug. If you later do split, those package boundaries are the seams you would cut along, so the work isn't wasted.

## When I'd change the recommendation

Split, at least partially, if one or more of these is true:

- **Release coupling is the measured bottleneck:** teams regularly wait days to ship because of other teams' changes, and flags plus trunk-based deploys haven't fixed it.
- **Cadence or compliance differs sharply:** for example, a regulated checkout flow next to a marketing surface that ships ten times a day.
- **You need a framework migration:** you want to run old and new side by side.
- **Product areas are truly separable:** there is little shared state, users rarely cross between them in a session, and the teams are in different orgs or time zones.
- **You expect to grow well past five teams** and can fund a platform team.

Even then, extract the one or two areas with the strongest case behind a thin shell, on a single React version and a single design system, rather than converting everything.

## Suggested next step

Ask each team for its top three sources of delivery friction and tag each as build speed, ownership or coupling, release coordination, or runtime isolation. If most land in the first two, do the modular monolith work. If release coordination dominates even with flags and continuous deploy in place, you have a real case for extracting that area.
